name: Ubud Monkey Forest
label: Monkey Forest
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Monkey Forest' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Monkey Forest nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9732447: large area 'Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary' (809 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Forest sanctuary with temples, mossy statues and macaques.

text.description:
Ubud Monkey Forest is a village-owned sanctuary in Padangtegal, Ubud, where tall trees, mossy stonework and a large troop of Balinese long-tailed macaques share the same few hectares. It covers about 10 hectares and has at least 115 tree species. As of 2023 about 1,260 macaques lived here. Three Hindu temples stand inside, all thought to date from around 1350. The place is still part of local spiritual life, so some areas are closed to visitors. That mix of jungle, old carved stone and animal life is why it photographs so well, and why a gentle, unhurried approach gets the best pictures.

Frame the stone entrance sign with the street's cafés and galleries around it, so the picture says where you are before you go in. Inside, two other spots are worth a frame. The stone bridge with dragon-headed railings over the ravine looks good with jungle and mossy statues at either end. The carved gateway of Pura Dalem Agung Padangtegal sits among the trees, and you shoot it from just outside, as the inner courtyard is for worshippers.

The macaques have lost their fear of people and may grab bags or climb on visitors. Keep your distance, avoid eye contact and never offer food. Let your zoom do the work rather than stepping closer.
text.geographic_location: In Padangtegal, in the Ubud area of Bali.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops here, so head into Ubud and make your way to Jalan Monkey Forest, then go to the southern end of the street near the main entrance. Look for the stone entrance sign. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the entrance sign and the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole entrance and the shopfronts. Inside, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for monkeys and carved details, so you never need to get close.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Monkey Forest (near the main entrance at the southern end of the street). The stone sign at the sanctuary entrance with the street's cafés and galleries nearby, giving a sense of place before going inside. From here the sanctuary lies to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the stone sign off-centre, leaving the street and shopfronts as context. If you want something different, the dragon-headed stone bridge over the ravine works well framed by jungle. The temple gateway of Pura Dalem Agung Padangtegal is best shot from just outside the gate, with the trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the sign or the monkey's face, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright patches between the trees don't wash out. For moving monkeys, hold the shutter for a burst or use Live Photos and pick the best frame. Portrait mode works for a monkey sitting still, but only from a safe distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The street outside is a quieter option than the forest itself.

text.access_note: The street outside is open to anyone, but entry to the sanctuary is paid and parts of it, including the sacred temple areas, are closed to visitors, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Bright gaps in the tree canopy can make photos taken under the trees look patchy, so lowering exposure helps.
Burst mode or Live Photos make it easier to catch a moving monkey at the right moment.

name: Ubud Palace
label: Ubud Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Raya Ubud' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Raya Ubud nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/284575978: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puri Saren Agung Ubud Palace' (72 m across).
notes: Royal palace in the heart of Ubud with traditional Balinese gates and courtyards.

text.description: Ubud Palace, officially Puri Saren Agung, was the official residence of Ubud's royal family, and the enclosure in front is also a residence for the royal family. It sits right on the main road in the town centre, and the palace front can be seen from the street. The picture is the front of the palace: carved walls, tall gates and detailed stonework, all in traditional Balinese style. The present palace dates from the reign of Tjokorda Putu Kandel (1800–1823). It was badly damaged in the 1917 earthquake, quickly restored, and opened to foreign guests in 1928. Many of the stone carvings are the work of the local artist I Gusti Nyoman Lempad. The palace is also known for its traditional dance shows, and the main pavilion usually hosts them at night. From the pavement opposite you can fit the whole frontage in one shot, then step closer for the detail. Look for the symmetry of the gates and the texture of the carved stone. Keep your phone steady and keep an eye on passing traffic and other visitors. Some areas inside may be ticketed, and photography can be restricted in sacred areas and during live performances, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Ubud, on the main road, Jalan Raya Ubud. The palace is the large royal compound on this stretch, with its private family temple, Pura Marajan Agung, to the north.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Ubud and ask your taxi or hired scooter to stop on Jalan Raya Ubud by the palace. Look for the carved walls and tall gates. Cross to the pavement directly opposite the front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the palace front as you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the full gates and walls in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the carvings and gate details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Raya Ubud (on the pavement directly across from the palace front, framing the carved walls and towering gates). The palace front with its ornately carved walls and tall gates, seen from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the gate with the centre of the frame so the symmetry looks tidy. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Include some of the carved wall at the edges to show the scale. For a different view, the Candi Bentar split gateway and the wooden Kul-Kul drum tower are both worth a look if you can reach them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the carved stonework to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring down bright sky so the carvings stay detailed. Take a few frames in case people walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a good bet for softer light and fewer people on the pavement. If you stay for the evening dance, remember that photography can be restricted during live performances, so ask first.

text.access_note: The palace front can be seen from the street, but some areas inside may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning usually gives softer light and fewer people on the pavement.
Traffic and other visitors pass along the pavement opposite the palace front.
Some areas inside the palace may need a ticket and photography can be restricted in sacred areas and during live dance performances.

name: Goa Gajah
label: Goa Gajah
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Goa Gajah' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1153609086: the OpenStreetMap point 'Goa Gajah cave'.
notes: Ancient cave sanctuary with a carved demon-mouth entrance and bathing pools.

text.description:
Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave, is a carved stone sanctuary set in a green hollow near Bedulu village. The cave mouth is framed by a crowded carving of a menacing face, thought to ward off evil spirits. The site is generally dated to the 9th to 11th centuries, and it mixes Hindu and Buddhist imagery. The cave was rediscovered by Dutch archaeologists in 1923, but the bathing pools were not uncovered until 1954.

The bathing pools make the best phone photo. Seven women statues hold water pitchers there, representing seven holy rivers, though one statue was lost in an earthquake. Stone spouts and figures sit in a tidy symmetrical row, with garden behind. A step or two higher than the pool level, both rows of spouts fit into one frame, and the repeating shapes suit a straight-on, centred shot.

The entrance to the cave is reached only by walking down a long flight of stairs, so wear comfortable shoes. The pools are the busiest corner, so arriving early gives you a cleaner frame. This is a working sacred place, so ask before photographing worshippers, don't block the doorway for long poses, and keep the flash off around people praying. If you also want the full demon face over the doorway, take that shot as well, and the older ruins and water in the valley below make a quieter third picture.
text.geographic_location: Goa Gajah is in Bedulu village, in Gianyar, on the south-eastern edge of the Ubud area, about 5 km from central Ubud. The site lies down a flight of stairs from the village entrance.
text.directions_text: From central Ubud, head south-east towards Bedulu village, about 5 km away. Look for signs to Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave. From the entrance, walk down the stairs into the complex to reach the cave and the bathing pools. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the row of spouts and statues over the bathing pools. If the pools feel too tight to fit in one frame, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more) for details, such as a single carved figure or the demon face over the cave doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the symmetrical-spouts shot, walk from there to the steps above the bathing pools. From this higher angle the row of stone spouts and statues over the pools fits in one photo, with the green garden behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre yourself on the middle of the pools and turn on gridlines so both rows of spouts sit evenly either side. Keep the phone level so the symmetry reads clearly. For a second picture, walk to the cave doorway and frame the full carved demon face so the whole entrance fills the screen. The older ruins and water in the valley below the main site, at Tukad Pangkung, are another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone spouts to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright patches wash out the stone. Keep the flash off, because people may be praying nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is quieter, with fewer large groups at the pools than around midday.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed temple complex and a place of worship, where visitors in shorts are given a sarong; check the official site before you go for entry details and opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Bright patches can wash out the stone, so lowering the exposure slider slightly may help.
Standing a little higher on the steps lets a phone fit both rows of spouts in one frame (taken from the researched viewpoint notes).
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) may be needed if the pools are too tight to fit in one frame.

name: Campuhan Ridge Walk
label: Campuhan Ridge Walk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pura Gunung Lebah' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pura Gunung Lebah' (way/556447402): middle (100 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W1263132900 (Campuhan Ridge Walk): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Scenic ridge path with grass hills and valley views at sunrise.

text.description: The Campuhan Ridge Walk is a paved path that runs along a ridge in Ubud, between tall grass with the valley beyond. It photographs well because the path gives you a natural leading line, and the grass and the open countryside beyond give you plenty of depth. From the entrance you can shoot the temple's carved walls and its tiered meru shrines, with the start of the ridge path running along beside them. Guides describe the entrance as a good place for pictures. One guide notes the temple was under renovation, so you can photograph the exterior but not go inside. That may have changed, so treat it as a guide only. Once you have your temple shots, walk north along the path. The classic view is the paved path between tall grass, framed by two palm trees, with the valley beyond. If you want a wider panorama of countryside and rice fields, Karsa Kafe at the northern end is another recommended spot, though it is a longer walk from here. Take the temple pictures first, then the path, and leave time to stop and look around as you go.
text.geographic_location: The walk is on the Campuhan ridge in Ubud, and its southern start is marked by the temple Pura Gunung Lebah. The point on the map is further north along the ridge path.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport information for this spot. From there the subject point on the map is to the north along the ridge path, about 1 km (985 m) on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the temple entrance, so the carved walls and meru towers fit in without you stepping back into the road or path. Use the default lens (1x) for the path and palm trees, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out carved details or compress the layers of the valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Pura Gunung Lebah (temple entrance at the southern start of the walk, shooting the carved walls). The temple's carved walls and tiered meru shrines, with the start of the ridge path beside them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the temple wall on one third of the frame, with the path leading off along the other. Keep the phone level so the walls and meru towers don't lean. Later, on the ridge, line the paved path up as a leading line between the tall grass and the two palm trees. For a wide view of fields and valley, Karsa Kafe at the northern end is the other recommended spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the carved stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it doesn't wash out. Try a Live Photo on the path, as grass moving in the breeze can look nice in motion. Panorama mode suits the valley, if you hold the phone upright and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, lower light and fewer people on the path, so choose one of those if you can.

text.access_note: Pura Gunung Lebah is a place of worship, so dress modestly and respect any signs, and as it may be closed for renovation, check the official site or local signs before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ridge path is paved and runs between tall grass with the valley beyond.
Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and fewer people on the walk.
Dressing modestly is expected at a Balinese temple.
Pura Gunung Lebah may still be under renovation, which comes from a single guide and may be out of date.

name: Ubud Market
label: Ubud Art Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Puri Saren Agung' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Puri Saren Agung' (way/284575978): middle (72 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W238194819 (Ubud Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Colourful traditional market with crafts and souvenirs opposite the palace.

text.description: Ubud Market sits on the main road in the centre of Ubud, with stalls and shopfronts packed along the street. It photographs well because there is always something going on: shoppers, scooters and colourful goods spilling out towards the road. The classic picture is taken from the front of the Puri Saren Agung palace, looking across Jalan Raya Ubud to the market's frontage and stalls. If you want a second angle, try Jalan Raya Ubud for the main corner frontage, where the newer multi-storey buildings mix with passing street life. Jalan Karna gives a close, colourful view down a narrow lane lined with stalls. Early morning is when local trade happens, before the souvenir stalls open, and that can make a quieter, more everyday shot. Keep your phone in a pocket or wrist strap while you walk through the lanes. Take a few frames from the palace side first, then cross over for details.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Ubud, across Jalan Raya Ubud from the front of the Puri Saren Agung palace.
text.directions_text: From the middle of Ubud, walk to the front of Puri Saren Agung on Jalan Raya Ubud. The market is across the road to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the classic frontage shot. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrow lane on Jalan Karna, where you cannot step back. Try 2x for close-ups of stalls and goods.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Puri Saren Agung (front of the palace, looking across Jalan Raya Ubud toward the market). The market's frontage and stalls, framed from the palace side of the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the market frontage along the lower third, with the street activity in the foreground. For a second view, walk to Jalan Raya Ubud for the corner frontage, or into Jalan Karna for a close view down the lane of stalls. Tap the brightest stall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on a stall, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky washes out. Try a Live Photo to capture people passing. In the narrow lane, hold the phone steady with both hands and take several frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when local trade is under way before the souvenir stalls open.

text.access_note: The market is an open public place and the palace front is a free public compound; check on the day for any closures or restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Jalan Raya Ubud carries traffic, so take care when stepping into the road for a photo.
Narrow lanes such as Jalan Karna are tight enough that the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps.

name: Pura Taman Saraswati
label: Saraswati Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Café Lotus' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cafe Lotus' (way/445459695): middle (22 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/238194818: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saraswati Temple' (113 m across).
notes: Temple famous for its lotus pond and carved gateway.

text.description:
Pura Taman Saraswati, also called the Ubud Water Palace, is a Balinese Hindu temple dedicated to Sarasvati, the goddess of learning, literature and art. It is best known for the lotus pond and water garden around the outer area, with frangipani trees along the edges and a straight stone approach lined with carved figures from Hindu stories. Beyond them stand three red-brick gateways, with the tallest in the middle between two frangipani trees. The temple was designed by the Balinese sculptor and architect I Gusti Nyoman Lempad, and it was built between 1951 and 1952.

It photographs well because the water gives you reflections and layers: flowers or leaves in front, the pond in the middle, and the gateways and carved roofs behind. An alternative viewpoint for a phone is the terrace at Café Lotus, on the western side of the pond. From there you look slightly down and across the water to the temple, which is a wider and calmer view than the one from the walkway. The pond may look rather bare outside the lotus season, which guides give as roughly June to September, so the temple itself may need to be the star of your photo. If you want a different angle, the stone causeway gives a symmetrical frame with the gate at the far end. The larger pond can also be seen from the roadside along Jalan Raya Ubud.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Ubud. The pond can be seen from the roadside along Jalan Raya Ubud.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops here, so head on foot for the centre of Ubud and look for the large lotus pond, which can be seen from Jalan Raya Ubud. Café Lotus is a separate viewpoint on the western side of the pond. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of pond, gateways and roofs. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the gates and carvings, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground water or leaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Café Lotus (western side of the lotus pond, from the cafe terrace). An elevated, wider view across the pond toward the temple, a different angle from the walkway. Guides rate it as the best view over the ponds and the temple, but it is a paid spot, so expect to buy something while you are there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water in the lower third and the temple gateways along the upper line. Keep the lines of the roofs level. For a second angle, walk the stone causeway for a symmetrical shot, or shoot from the roadside along Jalan Raya Ubud for the larger pond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the water does not turn white. Take a few shots, with and without people in the frame, and use Live Photos if you would like a moving shot of ripples.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend sunset or golden hour for this view. The lotus flowers are said to bloom roughly from June to September.

text.access_note: The temple grounds are a ticketed place of worship and photography inside the main temple is restricted, so check the official site before you go for current prices, opening hours and dress rules; the Café Lotus terrace needs a purchase.
claims_not_in_sources: Placing the water in the lower third and keeping roof lines level is a general composition suggestion.
Lowering the exposure at sunset helps keep sky colour and avoid blown-out water; this is a general phone-camera suggestion.

name: Puri Lukisan Museum
label: Puri Lukisan
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9772789: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum Puri Lukisan' (148 m across).
notes: Oldest art museum in Bali, set in landscaped gardens.

text.description: Puri Lukisan is an art museum in Ubud devoted to traditional and modern Balinese painting and wood carving, with works from the 1930s onwards. The collection is shown across four buildings, set to the north, west, east and south: the Pitamaha Gallery, the Ida Bagus Made Gallery, the Wayang Gallery and the Founders Gallery. That layout gives you plenty to point a phone at without moving far. The architect and artist I Gusti Nyoman Lempad designed parts of the museum and painted the murals at the entrance to the North Building, so that doorway is worth a close look. Inside, highlights include Lempad's linear drawing the Dream of Dharmawangsa and Anak Agung Gde Sobrat's painting of a Balinese market, which was shown at the museum's opening. It photographs well because you can mix wide views of the buildings with close shots of carved and painted detail. Start with a wide frame of one building, then step closer for a mural, a doorway or a carved figure. Take a few seconds to tap on your subject so the focus is sharp, and slide the exposure down a touch if bright sky is washing out the walls. Rules on taking photos inside the galleries can differ from the grounds, so check the official site before you go and follow any signs once you are in.
text.geographic_location: The buildings stand around it on the north, west, east and south sides.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops serve Ubud, so start from the middle of Ubud town. Go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Museum Puri Lukisan. Once through the entrance, head for the middle of the site, where the phone icon on the map is marked. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most shots. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a whole building, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for murals and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, turn slowly and the buildings on the north, west, east and south sides come into view in turn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the building edges straight to avoid leaning walls. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for a full building, then the default lens (1x) for doorways. Move closer, or use 2x or more, for the murals at the North Building entrance. Keep your phone steady and hold it level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then slide the exposure down slightly to keep detail in light walls. For carvings and paintings, tap on the detail itself so focus is sharp. Portrait mode can suit a single carved figure if the background is busy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Midday sun can make deep shadows around doorways and roofs, so use the exposure slider if that happens.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so entry may be ticketed and photography rules inside may differ; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ubud has no Underground, tram or train stops, so taxi or scooter is the usual way to reach the museum.
The middle of the museum site has enough open space to stand and turn between the buildings.
Photography rules inside the galleries may differ from those in the grounds.
Morning and late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
Midday sun can cause deep shadows around doorways and roofs.

name: Blanco Renaissance Museum
label: Blanco Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2031494034: the OpenStreetMap point 'Don Antonio Blanco Museum'.
notes: Eccentric home and gallery of the painter Antonio Blanco.

text.description: The Blanco Renaissance Museum is an art museum in Ubud, devoted to the work of the painter Antonio Blanco. It opened on 28 December 1998. For a phone photographer it makes a simple stop, and you can take a few different pictures in a short visit: a wide shot of the building, a closer shot of whatever details catch your eye, and a portrait of a friend or family member with the building behind them. The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum, so you are photographing the place from the spot itself. Start with the whole building and take a step back if you can, so it does not get cut off at the edges. Then move in and look for textures, patterns and colours that reflect the museum's focus on the art of Antonio Blanco. Keep your phone steady against a wall or railing if the light is low. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go, as access and photography rules for the galleries may differ from the outside. Be considerate of other visitors when you stop to take pictures, and keep to any signs you see.
text.geographic_location: In Ubud, on the island of Bali, Indonesia. The museum is also known as the Don Antonio Blanco Museum.
text.directions_text: No railway or tram stops are listed near this spot, so start from the centre of Ubud and get to the museum by road. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there is no further walk: about 0 minutes on foot. Ask for the Blanco Renaissance Museum, or the Don Antonio Blanco Museum. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building as you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the building and cannot fit it all in. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details that catch your eye.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building with the vertical lines so it does not lean. Take one wide frame of the whole building, then one closer detail shot. If a friend is with you, try portrait mode with the building behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls do not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is usually kinder than midday, when the light is harsh and shadows are strong.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so entry may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.
